#10243. A New Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents (EVA)

Conversational voice agents present a distinct evaluation challenge: they must simultaneously satisfy two objectives — accuracy (completing the user's task correctly and faithfully) and conversational experience (doing so naturally, concisely, and in a way appropriate for spoken interaction). These objectives are deeply intertwined: mishearing a confirmation code renders perfect LLM reasoning meaningless, a wall of options overwhelms a caller who can't skim spoken output, and delayed responses can pass every accuracy check while remaining unusable in practice. Existing frameworks treat these as separate concerns — evaluating task success or conversational dynamics, but not both.

We introduce EVA, an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that evaluates complete, multi-turn spoken conversations using a realistic bot-to-bot architecture. EVA produces two high-level scores, EVA-A (Accuracy) and EVA-X (Experience), and is designed to surface failures along each dimension. EVA is the first to jointly score task success and conversational experience. We release EVA with an initial airline dataset of 50 scenarios covering flight rebooking, cancellation handling, vouchers, and more — the first in a planned series of domains.

We also provide benchmark results for 20 cascade and audio-native systems, such as speech-to-speech (S2S) models and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs). Our biggest finding is that there is a consistent Accuracy-Experience tradeoff; agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa.

The field currently lacks a framework that evaluates the full quality of voice agent interactions, as most existing efforts assess individual components in isolation. For example, AudioBench, SD-Eval, VoxEval, Kimi-Audio-Evalkit, VoiceBench and VoxDialogue evaluate core speech understanding capabilities for Speech-to-Text (STT) — transcription, paralinguistics, acoustic cues — but remain confined to single-turn, non-interactive settings. On the other hand, EmergentTTS-Eval and SHEET assess perceived speech quality using subjective listening tests (e.g., Mean Opinion Score). Beyond speech perception, FD-Bench, Talking Turns, Full-Duplex-Bench provide deeper analyses of conversational dynamics — interruptions, backchanneling, turn-taking — yet evaluate these in isolation from task-oriented tool use, leaving the relationship between dialogue quality and agentic capability unexamined. More recent efforts, notably VoiceAgentBench and CAVA, take steps towards evaluating the agentic capabilities of commercial voice agent systems, including tool-calling and complex instruction-following. However, these voice-agentic capabilities are not evaluated within complete conversational workflows that voice agents must navigate in practice: from initial user request through multi-step tool orchestration to final task resolution.

The lack of frameworks that jointly capture accuracy and experience underscores the need for a framework that treats voice agent quality as an integrated whole. This means evaluating not only whether the task succeeded, but whether the agent communicated accurately, concisely, and naturally throughout, and surfacing how these dimensions trade off against one another in realistic deployment conditions.

End-to-end evaluation reveals interaction dynamics that are not apparent at the component level: whether the agent interrupts users during natural pauses in speech, whether it recovers smoothly when a user corrects a transcription error, or whether high latency disrupts the conversational flow enough to prompt users to repeat themselves or abandon the task entirely.

EVA simulates multi-turn spoken conversations over live audio in which the agent must invoke appropriate tools, adhere to task-specific policies, and reach a deterministically verifiable end state. EVA evaluates voice agents using a bot-to-bot audio architecture composed of five core components:

User Simulator — A conversational AI configured with a specific goal and persona that plays the role of a caller. It operates in audio using high-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, ensuring the evaluation captures representative speech-understanding challenges in natural-sounding conversational speech and realistic turn-taking dynamics.

Voice Agent — The voice agent being evaluated, built with Pipecat, an open-source Python framework for real-time voice applications. EVA supports both cascade architectures (STT → LLM → TTS) and audio-native models (S2S or LALM → TTS).

Tool Executor — The engine that provides deterministic, reproducible tool responses via custom Python functions. It dynamically queries and modifies a predefined per-scenario database.

Validators — A set of validation metrics that check that conversations are complete and that the user faithfully reproduced the intended behavior and speech, with no human annotation required. Any conversation that fails in this validation step is regenerated, ensuring that only valid, correctly executed conversations enter evaluation. This stands in contrast to approaches that rely on post-hoc human labeling to identify simulator errors.

Metrics Suite — A suite of metrics evaluates the voice agent using the conversation recording, transcript, and tool call logs.

Each test case (scenario) in our framework is an evaluation record, structured to make tests reproducible:

We release EVA with a synthetic airline dataset of 50 scenarios and 15 tools, spanning IRROPS rebooking, voluntary itinerary changes, cancellations, same-day standby, and compensation vouchers. Scenarios are designed to test temporal reasoning, policy-following, constraint satisfaction, and named-entity handling.

EVA evaluates voice agents across two fundamental dimensions, EVA-A for accuracy, and EVA-X for experience. EVA also includes a set of diagnostic metrics. Unlike the primary metrics, these are not used directly to compare or rank models — rather, they offer granular insight into why a model scores the way it does, helping identify and understand specific failure modes (e.g., ASR, speech synthesis, etc.). We report pass@k (the probability that at least one of k runs succeeds) and pass^k (the probability that all k runs succeed) across three trials per scenario (k = 3), capturing both peak performance and behavioral consistency.

EVA uses two evaluation methods: deterministic code-based metrics, which compute scores directly from structured data and are fast; and LLM-as-Judge metrics, which use Large Language Models (LLMs) to assess qualitative aspects of the conversation, or Large Audio Language Models (LALM) to evaluate speech directly. Each judge-based metric uses the model that performs best on a curated evaluation dataset for that specific metric.

Task completion alone is a necessary but insufficient measure of accuracy. An agent can reach the correct end state while fabricating a policy detail, misreading a confirmation code aloud, or hallucinating a flight number mid-conversation. These failures are invisible to a binary pass/fail check but directly harm users. EVA-A therefore measures three dimensions of accuracy:

Turn-taking timing matters, but it tells only part of the story. An agent can have perfect timing while overwhelming a caller with a wall of spoken options they cannot skim, or repeatedly asking for information already given. These failures degrade the experience without ever involving a mistimed response. EVA-X therefore measures three dimensions of experience:

We evaluated 20 systems — proprietary and open-source, cascade and audio-native — and find a consistent accuracy-experience tradeoff: agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa — a tradeoff invisible to benchmarks that score only task completion. No single configuration dominates both axes, confirming that accuracy and experience must be measured jointly.

Additionally, we identified named entity transcription as a dominant failure mode. A single misheard character can cascade into an authentication failure and a full conversation breakdown. Also, multi-step workflows break agents in predictable ways. Rebooking a flight while preserving ancillary services — seats, baggage — is the dominant complexity breaker across all configurations. Finally, we observed that additional calibration is needed for real-world use cases. The gap between pass@3 and pass^3 is substantial across all configurations. Even agents that can complete a task often cannot do so consistently, which is critical for real-world success.

EVA is designed to provide rigorous, end-to-end evaluation of conversational voice agents, but several limitations are important to acknowledge, across the framework, data, and metrics dimensions:

Metrics — LLM-as-judge models carry inherent biases and may favor certain response styles independent of quality, with additional risk of systematic bias when the evaluated and judge models share a provider. While we validate our judges against labeled datasets and report accuracy measurements on our website, these alignment scores do not eliminate systematic bias entirely. Additionally, task completion is measured as binary, which does not capture partial credits and may understate the relative quality of systems that fail gracefully versus catastrophically.

Simulation — The current release covers 50 English-language scenarios in a single domain (airline); results may not generalize to other domains, languages, or accents. Also, the user simulator may not perfectly replicate real caller behavior (e.g., disfluencies, hesitations, emotions) or guarantee full policy adherence.

Framework — The user simulator relies on a single commercial provider whose voice characteristics may systematically favor certain ASR systems, and the bot-to-bot pipeline — including audio format conversions and real-time audio interfaces — may not fully represent production deployments. Also, full reproduction requires commercial API access, and latency measurements will vary across providers and infrastructure.

On the evaluation side, we plan to add prosodic quality assessment (pronunciation, rhythm, expressiveness) — currently an open problem after finding very low alignment between LALM-as-Judge and human judgments. We also plan robustness testing under noisy conditions, diverse accents, multilingual users, and varied speaker behaviors, alongside affect-aware evaluation of how agents respond to user distress. In terms of data, we are developing additional domain datasets — each with distinct policy structures, named entity profiles, and conversational dynamics — and more complex scenarios involving compound requests, multi-step follow-ups, and longer conversational memory. On the tooling front, we will release a results and error analysis application that automatically identifies errors per metric and model, surfaces representative examples for exploration, and generates structured summaries of each model’s strengths and weaknesses. Finally, we intend to expand the leaderboard continuously to provide an up-to-date assessment of voice agent capabilities across the field.

View more details about limitations and our upcoming roadmap here.

Core contributors include Tara Bogavelli, Gabrielle Gauthier Melançon, Katrina Stankiewicz, Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Hoang Nguyen, Raghav Mehndiratta, and Hari Subramani.

We also thank Lindsay Brin, Akshay Kalkunte, Joseph Marinier, Jishnu Nair, and Aman Tiwari for their careful data review and thoughtful contributions to the framework, and Fanny Riols, Anil Madamala, Sridhar Nemala, and Srinivas Sunkara for their management, leadership, and support throughout. We also extend our thanks to the PAVA and CLAE ServiceNow teams, whose prior work on evaluations and voice agents provided valuable inspiration for this project.

Alice Huang, the person allegedly involved in an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has reportedly surfaced in Beijing, marking the first sighting of the Megaspeed executive since the scandal broke out. According to Bloomberg, it’s unclear when the suspected Chinese spy arrived in the capital or why she’s in the area, but she was last spotted leaving Singapore for Shanghai in 2025 after she was detained and questioned during the city-state’s investigation into the $2-billion smuggling case involving Megaspeed.

The Nvidia CEO is now under intense scrutiny after the revelation of his indiscretion with the Megaspeed executive, with Congress threatening to issue a subpoena if he does not respond to their invitation to “a joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. The FBI is also looking into the relationship between the head of the largest AI hardware company in the world and a person suspected of helping sanctioned Chinese companies secure hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips. Overnight, a second bombshell report claims that Jensen Huang was also involved in an extramarital affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Although the Chinese embassy in Washington has denied any links to Alice Huang, calling it nothing but “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing, there is speculation that she’s under the control of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is the primary agency that handles China’s foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. The U.S. intelligence community suggests that she may be passing on information to the MSS, but it remains unclear if she was specifically tasked by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang or if they were only leveraging her relationship with the Nvidia chief to get insights into the U.S. AI industry.

A deeper investigation into Alice Huang, known by her Chinese name as Huang Le, revealed that she supposedly worked in media before jumping into banking and finance. The Wall Street Journal reports that it’s unclear when she met her husband, Kang Wei, but the couple ran a private equity and investment management firm called Shanghai Hexi in 2016. This allowed the couple to invest in companies across industries, including gaming, pharmaceuticals, and, eventually, data centers and cloud computing.

The couple is known for riding trends and isn’t a stranger to scandals. Their firm, Shanghai Hexi, invested in gaming companies in the 2010s, especially when mobile gaming started to boom across the world, while Chinese regulators fined Kang and the company in 2018 for disclosure failures and other violations while it was in the midst of a takeover battle for a corporation. Kang’s moves in the gaming industry are what allowed him to meet Jensen Huang, which eventually led to a close relationship between the couple and the Nvidia chief. Sources told the WSJ that Kang apparently accepted Alice and Jensen’s extra-marital relationship, even sometimes jokingly telling people that she was Jensen’s “personal assistant.”

It seems that the couple is used to leveraging their relationships to gain business advantage, and with investments in AI data centers expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, Alice Huang’s “close” relationship with Jensen Huang put Shanghai Hexi in an excellent position to take advantage of the trend through Megaspeed and make big money. And with U.S. sanctions making it harder for competitors to acquire Nvidia chips, it appears that their access has turned into a gold mine for the company. But whether Alice Huang acted solely out of business interest with the supposed procurement of Nvidia chips or was leveraged by Chinese authorities to import these chips, the fact remains that $7.5 billion worth of banned chips reportedly made their way into China despite Washington’s efforts.

#10240. Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

#10238. Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon

Edge AI complements the cloud to bring the best AI experiences. These rely on a continuous flow of context and intelligence across both, working as a model cascade where information is captured and processed in the right place at the right time. Ultra-low-power models on the edge can continuously sense and respond in real time, while seamlessly handing off to larger on-device or cloud models when deeper reasoning is needed.

Still, building for the edge is much harder than it should be. While cloud infrastructure has converged around a few standard software stacks, the edge is split across hundreds of proprietary chip architectures and incompatible toolchains. For ML developers, this creates a heavy fragmentation tax, where you end up rewriting kernels, re-quantizing models, and debugging vendor-specific compilers for every chip you target.

Last year, Google Research introduced Coral NPU with a simple idea: an open hardware and software standard is the only way to unify the edge and unlock developer productivity and portability. Our standards based, ML-first RISC-V architecture paired with a reliable open-source toolchain gives developers confidence that their models will compile and run, letting teams optimize a model once and deploy it across different SoC vendors, devices, and power envelopes.

Today, we are reaching three major milestones in the Coral effort:

Fixing fragmentation at the edge takes more than publishing an instruction set. Historically, many edge accelerators were designed to hit high peak-compute numbers on spec sheets, leaving compiler teams to figure out software support later. In practice, unsupported neural network layers fall back to a general-purpose CPU, which can hurt latency and drain the battery.

We designed the Coral NPU architecture and its compiler together from the start. Instead of chasing peak metrics, our focus is on energy-viable compute: helping to deliver the right performance at the right power envelope for your application.

Over the past year, we released the first three milestones of the 32-bit Coral NPU design: a C-programmable RISC-V scalar frontend for control flow (Milestone 1), an RVV v1.0 vector co-processor for SIMD operations (Milestone 2), and a tightly coupled memory subsystem with floating point support (Milestone 3). With this month's release of the Matrix Execution Unit (Milestone 4), the 32-bit architecture is complete.

Scalar and vector units are great for general control logic and signal processing, but modern ML workloads—from vision encoders to transformer attention layers—spend most of their time on 2D matrix-matrix (GEMM) and matrix-vector (GEMV) multiplication. Running 2D matrix math on a 1D vector engine forces the chip to repeatedly load weights and activations from memory, which can mean spending more energy moving data than doing math.

Our Matrix Execution Unit leverages the RISC-V VME specification (formally part of the Zvt family) to address this need and uses a dedicated outer-product multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine. Because an outer-product engine computes a full 2D tile of operations in a single cycle (256 MACs per cycle), it reuses weights and activations directly inside local registers. This brings quadratic throughput scaling to the core, configurable for up to 1 TOPS.

Having a dedicated matrix engine in a sub-10 mW envelope changes what developers can build on a small battery. Rather than stopping at simple keyword spotting or basic motion detection, devices can run continuous, multimodal workloads, including compact transformer models like Gemma, real-time voice translation on wearables, spatial audio filtering on hearables, and low-latency visual perception on robots.

To help silicon teams bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub.

To make the hardware easy to target without writing custom assembly, we are also releasing the v1.0 foundation of our open-source MLIR/IREE compiler toolchain.

With this stack, you can bring models from JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow through standard representations like StableHLO and TOSA. The compiler partitions workloads between the host CPU and the Coral NPU core, handles operator fusion, tiles matrices to fit local SRAM and matrix accumulators, and progressively lowers workloads directly to Coral NPU scalar, RVV v1.0 vector, and VME matrix instructions. Alongside our open-source MPACT simulator and reference FPGA design, hardware and software teams can benchmark models and tune silicon configurations before a chip ever goes to fabrication.

Turning an open standard into commercial silicon takes collaboration across the entire semiconductor value chain. To help silicon partners bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub, and we are partnering with VeriSilicon on the design implementation and verification (DV) to ensure turnkey readiness for silicon tape-outs. We are also working with GlobalFoundries on their 12LP+ FinFET process - accelerating core timing by 70%, and reducing standard-cell area by up to 15% across RTL iterations, with ongoing evaluation of 12LP+ ultra low-power libraries for the Matrix Execution Unit.

On the commercial silicon side, our collaboration with Synaptics shows how quickly this open standard translates into real hardware across very different power budgets without splitting the software experience.

At Synaptics Tech Day (October 20, 2026), Synaptics is launching three commercial silicon and hardware products built on Coral NPU technology and supported by the open IREE/MLIR toolchain:

Because both product families build on the same architecture and compiler foundation, ML teams can optimize a model once and deploy it to a milliwatt-class wearable (Coralboard SR) or a 1 TOPS board (Coralboard SL) using the same workflow. Developed in collaboration with hardware and System-on-Module partner Grinn, the Coralboard lineup also gives teams a direct path from devkit prototyping to commercial production hardware.

With our 32-bit architecture and v1.0 compiler stack in place, we are already working on the next phase of the roadmap, including a 64-bit Coral NPU architecture and CHERI support for security.

Whether you are designing a custom edge SoC, working on ML compilers, or deploying models to wearables and robotics, Coral NPU can help give you an open path from model to silicon. Here is where you can get started:

We would like to thank the core contributors and leadership team for this work, particularly Billy Rutledge, Ben Laurie, Derek Chow, Shaked Flur, Alex Van Damme, Bilal Khan, David Gao, Gregory Kielian, Julian Mullings-Black, Khaled Talukder, Lun Dong, Matthew Wilson, Michael Hoang, Murali Vijayaraghavan, Naveen Dodda, Roman Lewkow, Stefan Hall, Tor Jeremiassen, Yenkai Wang, Manya Dasari, Akib Uddin, Divya Pandya, Steve He, Preeti Singh, Anthony Phalen, Hans Rempel, Esmeralda Cardenas, Isha Mishra, Katy Zima, Resham Parikh, Hannah Bayer Rushing, Taylor Montgomery, Kai Yick, Srikanth Muroor, Cindy Liu, Bangfei Pan, Alec Go, Geoff Stirling, Robin Dua, Gaurav Arora, Steve Goldberg, Francesco Visin, Gus Martins, Ian Ballantyne, Kat Black, Ravin Kumar, Tris Warkentin, Avinatan Hassidim, Jay Yagnik, Katherine Chou, Shahram Izadi, and Yossi Matias.

Dbrand says it was tasked with developing another strap option for the Fitbit Air; thus, the rugged and modern Pulse band was born.

Google has a small collection of official accessory partners it works with to create third-party add-ons for its products under the “Made for Google” umbrella. Dbrand happens to be one of them, and has been since the launch of the Pixel 7.

Available starting today, the Dbrand Pulse band launches for the Fitbit Air starting at $34.95. It’s the first official Made for Google strap that fits the Fitbit Air. Dbrand claims Google tasked them with developing a new band because the Fitbit Air has been such a major success. Hopefully, we see more Made for Google brands release bands for the Fitbit Air. This is a great first step.

Dbrand’s Pulse band for the Fitbit Air is available on the company’s website, starting today.

#10236. TRL v1.0: Post-Training Library Built to Move with the Field

We’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is. What started as a research codebase has become a dependable library people build on, with clearer expectations around stability. This isn't just a version bump. It reflects the reality that TRL now powers production systems, and embraces that responsibility.

TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods. But coverage isn’t the goal by itself. What matters is making these methods easy to try, compare, and actually use in practice. The design of the library wasn’t decided upfront. It is the result of years of iteration — the first commit goes back more than six years — and it has been shaped by everything the field threw at it: new algorithms, new models, shifting paradigms. Over time, this pressure forced the codebase toward a very specific design. Parts of it might look unusual at first, but like in many evolutionary codebases, they exist for a reason.

TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still. So the question is not how to design the perfect abstraction. It is how to make stable software in a domain that keeps invalidating its own assumptions. This is what we tried to solve in TRL v1.0, and this post explains how.

Post-training has not evolved as a smooth refinement of one recipe. It has moved through successive centers of gravity, each changing not just the objective, but the shape of the stack.

PPO [Schulman et al., (2017); Ziegler et al., (2019)] made one architecture look canonical: a policy, a reference model, a learned reward model, sampled rollouts, and an RL loop.

Then DPO-style methods such as the original DPO [Rafailov et al., (2023)], ORPO [Hong et al., (2024)], and KTO [Ethayarajh et al., (2024)] cut through that stack: preference optimization could work without a separate reward model, value model, or any online RL. Components that had looked fundamental suddenly looked optional.

RLVR-style methods such as GRPO [Shao et al., (2024)] shifted the center again. On tasks like math, code, and tool use, rewards often come from verifiers or deterministic checks rather than learned reward models. Sampling and rollouts matter again, but the objects in the loop are no longer quite the ones PPO libraries were designed around.

The lesson is not just that methods change. The definition of the core keeps changing with them. Strong assumptions here have a short half-life. This is probably why no post-training library is really stable yet.

So what does it mean to build a library for a field that won't sit still? The answer is counterintuitive: don't try to capture the essence of what's stable today. Instead, design around what could change. Reward models illustrate why: they looked essential in PPO, became optional in DPO, and came back as verifiers in RLVR methods — structures that could be deterministic functions rather than learned models. Any abstraction built around their original form would have been obsolete twice over by now. The library survives by recognizing that strong assumptions have a short life, and by making that changeability central to how the codebase is organized.

This is the environment in which TRL is downloaded 3 million times a month, and in which major downstream projects treat it as stable infrastructure. The field keeps shifting the ground, and at the same time, those users need things not to break.

TRL didn’t make a deliberate decision to become a library. It found out it already was one. Projects like Unsloth and Axolotl — with thousands of users between them — had built directly on top of TRL’s trainers and APIs. A breaking change in TRL propagated instantly into their stacks. A renamed argument, a shifted default, a restructured output — any of these became someone else’s incident. The shift had already happened. v1.0 is the moment TRL acknowledged it explicitly.

The unusual thing about TRL’s stability model is not what it guarantees, it is what it tolerates alongside those guarantees. Stable and experimental coexist within the same package, with explicitly different contracts. The stable core follows semantic versioning. The experimental layer makes no such promises — it is where new methods land while they are still being evaluated, and where the API can move fast to keep up with the field.

This isn’t a compromise. It’s a response to a specific constraint: the field produces new methods faster than any of them can earn stability. Refusing to add immature methods would make TRL irrelevant within months. Adding them all to stable would break every downstream project every time an algorithm turned out not to work as expected.

Promotion from experimental to stable isn’t automatic. What matters is the ratio between maintenance cost and actual usage. Some methods earn their place because the community uses them heavily. Others become viable because we can make them cheap enough to maintain — and the design of the codebase is what makes that possible.

In practice, the stable surface includes trainers for SFT, DPO, Reward modeling, RLOO, and GRPO, along with their close variants. The experimental surface is broader and moves faster; for an up-to-date view, the best reference is the TRL documentation.

The breaking changes needed to reach v1.0 were distributed deliberately across the 0.x releases. Migration from the last 0.x version is minimal — see the migration guide.

In a domain where patterns keep changing, the temptation is to build flexible abstractions that can accommodate anything. Our answer was the opposite: limit abstractions to the strict minimum — while recognizing that this “minimum” is almost always overestimated.

In practice, this translates into a very local approach to code:

The goal is not to eliminate structure altogether — shared utilities still exist — but to avoid imposing abstractions where the domain itself is not yet stable. For instance, rather than defining a common base class for offline trainers, we prefer independent implementations when their future evolution is uncertain.

Judges are a good example of what happens when we don’t follow this principle. Early on, we introduced a Judge abstraction to unify the various ways of evaluating model outputs. It looked reasonable at the time. In practice, it was never really used — the abstraction didn’t match how people actually approached evaluation, and it added indirection without adding value. It still lives in the repo, mostly as legacy. In hindsight, shipping the concrete implementations without the unifying abstraction would have served users better.

This approach favors explicit and modifiable usage over rigid frameworks: less magic, but more control. It comes with an obvious cost: code duplication. While often seen as an anti-pattern, in this context it has proven not only acceptable, but effective. Contrary to intuition, it remains manageable in practice with a small but consistent discipline: keeping deltas between implementations minimal and avoiding unnecessary divergence. Like in the Transformers design philosophy, we accept duplication and local explicitness by design. The motivations largely coincide, with some nuance in focus.

This is easier to see than to describe. Compare RLOO and GRPO: large parts of their implementation are duplicated almost line for line. That is not accidental, and it is not dead weight. These methods are close enough that keeping their code paths aligned makes them easier to read, easier to evolve, and cheaper to maintain.

The goal of this comparison is not to argue that TRL should be judged as best on every axis. It should not. Some systems are built for maximum throughput (like PipelineRL), some are optimized for a narrower slice of the problem (like LLaMA-Factory), and some offer a more opinionated development experience in a specific environment (like Tinker). TRL occupies a different place in the ecosystem: it is a general-purpose post-training library that tries to keep the API and the code as simple as the domain allows, while combining broad method coverage, deep Hugging Face integration, a relatively low infrastructure burden, and an explicit stability contract.

Libraries like Unsloth and Axolotl are not included here because they build on top of TRL rather than sitting beside it in the comparison; in that sense, many of their users are also TRL users indirectly.

Some rows are factual (GitHub stars, Last release, Last commit), others are qualitative judgments (Semver stability).

Taken together, these comparisons point to a clear role for TRL: a general-purpose library designed to keep breadth, simplicity, integration, and stability in the same place. Its full downstream footprint is hard to measure, since most deployments are private and reverse dependencies are largely invisible, but the available signals already show that TRL operates at a distinctly different scale.

By now, the logic of v1.0 should be clear: it is not a claim that post-training has stabilized. On the contrary, it is an acknowledgment that the field will keep shifting, and that we're confident that the library has the right shape to absorb whatever comes next. The question is not what comes after v1.0, but what’s next for v1.0.

Today, GRPO in TRL is primarily used through a synchronous loop: generate rollouts, score them, then step the optimizer. That shape is simple and dependable, but it ties throughput to the slowest stage and leaves performance on the table at scale.

The fix is conceptually simple: generation and training don't need to be lock-stepped. We already have an early asynchronous GRPO design, and the next step is to harden it. The core idea is to decouple generation and training, letting generation run continuously on dedicated inference resources while training consumes a steady stream of scored trajectories, with buffering, backpressure, and clear policy-version accounting. This improves utilization and scales across GPUs and nodes. Other libraries already offer forms of asynchronous RL, but bringing it to TRL would make this style of training available through broader integrations, simpler APIs, and a much lower barrier to adoption.

The next candidates include KTO and newer distillation trainers such as SDFT, SDPO, and possibly GOLD or GKD. As discussed in Section 2, before moving them to stable, the goal is to minimize code differences across implementations and monitor sustained community interest relative to maintenance cost.

TRL supports large-scale training, including multi-node runs and larger models; the next step is to make this path significantly more robust and easier to operate in production. That includes stronger guarantees around distributed stability, clearer scaling defaults, and deeper support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), especially expert parallelism, where routing, load balancing, and memory behavior become critical.

Training is still too often driven by vibes. Loss curves go down, reward curves go up, a few samples look better than before, and people convince themselves the run is working. When it fails, they scroll through logs, compare runs by eye, and guess. That is already a weak interface for humans. For agents, it is worse: it is barely an interface at all.

One of the most important directions for TRL is to make training legible to software, not just to people. That means going beyond dashboards and raw metrics to produce explicit signals: is the policy improving, collapsing, over-optimizing the verifier, drifting off-distribution, or plateauing? The goal is for TRL to surface these patterns automatically, explain them clearly, and turn them into actions.

The plan is to embed heuristics directly into the training loop and emit structured, actionable warnings — the kind a beginner can act on immediately and an agent can parse:

Not just logging what happened — reasoning about what it means and what to do next. Useful for beginners who need guardrails, and for agents that need a training stack they can actually automate.

Post-training doesn't converge. It shifts, and the next shift is already coming.

v1.0 is not a claim that things have settled. It's an acknowledgment that they haven't yet, and a commitment that the library can be relied on anyway. Six years of evolving alongside the field — and alongside the hundreds of contributors who made it possible — shaped a design we're confident is ready for what comes next, whatever that turns out to be. The community and the downstream projects had already assumed that stability — v1.0 makes it real.

Migration from the last 0.x release is minimal, and the migration guide covers everything. If you're new, now is a good time to start.

Austrian cooling outfit Noctua is officially rolling its new NT-CP1 AM5/4 Carbice carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM4 and AM5 processors into the retail market. After announcing its partnership with advanced nanotechnology company Carbice back in June 2026, the premium thermal pad can now be purchased for $24.95 in the US and €24.95 in the European region.

Conventional thermal pastes and most thermal pads gradually lose performance over time due to pump-out, delamination, cracking, and other forms of degradation. However, Noctua says that its new NT-CP1 thermal pad takes a different approach. It makes use of Carbice's vertically-aligned carbon nanotube technology, originally developed for high thermal reliability in aerospace systems. The carbon nanotubes gradually conform to microscopic imperfections of a CPU’s IHS over hundreds to thousands of thermal cycles.

This allows heat transfer performance to improve during the initial activation period rather than gradually deteriorating. The thermal pad can also maintain stable, maintenance-free performance for years once the initial activation phase is complete. Thus, making it a suitable option for users who want consistent thermal performance without having to periodically replace degraded thermal paste.

"Carbice pads offer a unique combination of ultimate performance stability and convenient installation. This makes the NT-CP1 the perfect choice for everyone who’s looking for a thermal pad that’s super easy to apply and never needs to be replaced," said Noctua CEO Roland Mossig in a press note.

Unlike conventional carbon or graphite-based thermal pads, which can be brittle, slippery, and electrically conductive, the NT-CP1 features an aluminum backbone sandwiched between layers of carbon nanotubes. The surface is also protected by a nanoscale polymer coating, which Noctua says makes the pad more robust, easier to handle, and less likely to move during installation. The company recommends a simple peel, press, and peel installation process, while the slightly tacky coating helps keep the pad in place and offers electrical insulation as long as the polymer layer remains intact.

With an ultra-thin 90µm profile and precut 33x33mm size, the thermal pad fits both AM5 and AM4 socket processors. Noctua also highlights its manufacturing process, noting that the pad is produced in the US using recycled aluminum and waste carbon gas to grow the carbon nanotubes. The company claims that its manufacturing process is more energy-efficient compared to conventional graphite and graphene-based pads, while the aluminum structure allows the product to be recycled through standard aluminum recycling channels.

#10234. Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

To compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the plans page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid plans also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.
