#10197. Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. In my previous blogpost, I introduced the new multimodal capabilities, showing how to use embedding and reranker models that handle text, images, audio, and video. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to train or finetune these multimodal models on your own data.

As a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query. The resulting tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr demonstrates how much performance you can gain by finetuning on your own domain. On my evaluation data, the finetuned model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 compared to the base model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models I tested against, including models up to 4x its size.

If you're new to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first. For training text-only embedding, reranker, or sparse embedding models, see the Prior Blogposts section at the end.

General-purpose multimodal embedding models like Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B are trained on diverse data to perform well across a wide range of languages and tasks: image-text matching, visual question answering, document understanding, and more. But this generality means the model is rarely the best choice for any specific task.

Consider Visual Document Retrieval: given a text query like "What was the company's Q3 revenue?", the model must find the most relevant document screenshot from a corpus of thousands. This requires understanding document layouts, charts, tables, and text, which is a very different skill from e.g. matching pictures of shoes with product descriptions.

By finetuning on domain-specific data, the model can learn these specialized patterns. In my experiment, finetuning improved NDCG@10 from 0.888 to 0.947, ahead of every recent multimodal model I tested, including ones up to 4x larger.

Training multimodal Sentence Transformer models involves the same components as training text-only models:

The multimodal training pipeline uses the same SentenceTransformerTrainer as text-only training. The key difference is that your datasets contain images (or other modalities) alongside text, and the model's processor handles the image preprocessing automatically.

Let's walk through each component, using Visual Document Retrieval (matching text queries to document screenshots) as a running example.

The most common approach is to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model, or to start from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) checkpoint. The Transformer module automatically detects supported modalities from the model's processor.

To finetune an existing multimodal embedding model (e.g. one that already has a modules.json file), you can pass processor_kwargs and model_kwargs to control preprocessing and model loading respectively. processor_kwargs are passed directly to AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(...) (e.g., image resolution bounds: higher max_pixels means higher quality but more memory), while model_kwargs are passed to the appropriate AutoModel.from_pretrained(...) call (e.g., precision, attention implementation):

You can also start from a fresh VLM checkpoint that hasn't been trained for embeddings yet. Sentence Transformers will attempt to recognize the architecture, infer the supported modalities from the processor, and set up the appropriate forward method and pooling. If the automatic detection doesn't work perfectly for a particular model, the configuration in the saved sentence_bert_config.json can be edited to adjust modality settings, forward methods, and output handling:

In both cases, the Transformer module inspects the processor to determine which modalities are available, and Pooling is added automatically if needed. You can verify the supported modalities:

Instead of using a single VLM backbone, you can compose separate encoders for different modalities using the Router module. This lets you combine any existing encoders and route inputs to the appropriate one based on detected modality:

Since Router-based multimodal models use separate encoders per modality, their embedding spaces are initially unaligned. Training is required to align the spaces for meaningful cross-modal similarity. The Dense projection layer shown above helps map embeddings from different encoders into a shared space.

This approach is useful when you want to use lightweight, specialized encoders rather than a large VLM. You can also combine Router-based multimodality with task-based routing (e.g. different encoders for queries vs. documents) using route_mappings. See the Router documentation for advanced routing scenarios.

For this example, I use the tomaarsen/llamaindex-vdr-en-train-preprocessed dataset, a preprocessed English subset of llamaindex/vdr-multilingual-train. The source dataset was released alongside the Visual Document Retrieval Goes Multilingual blogpost by LlamaIndex, and consists of ~500k multilingual query-image samples collected from public internet PDFs, with queries synthetically generated using VLMs (gemini-1.5-pro and Qwen2-VL-72B). My preprocessed version filters to the 53,512 English samples and resolves 4 of the 16 ID-based hard negatives per sample into actual document screenshot images, so it can be used directly for training without further preprocessing:

The train config contains the first 10,000 samples, and the eval config contains the next 300 samples (a full config with all 53,512 samples is also available). For training, I select query, image, and negative_0 to form (anchor, positive, hard negative) triplets. Including additional hard negatives would likely improve the training signal, but each extra negative also increases memory usage and training time, so I stick with one. For evaluation, I keep all four hard negatives per query to build a more challenging retrieval corpus (more on that in the Evaluator section).

Just like text-only training, the dataset format must match your chosen loss function. The rules are the same:

For multimodal datasets, the inputs can contain:

The data collator automatically calls model.preprocess(), which detects the modality of each input and applies the appropriate preprocessing. No manual tokenization or image processing is needed.

Many Hugging Face datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers, allowing you to easily find them at https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers.

For this training, I use CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, a common choice for retrieval tasks. It accepts (query, positive) pairs with any number of additional hard negative columns, from 0 up to n, as long as each sample has the same number of negatives. During training, the loss pushes each query's similarity to its positive up and its similarity to every negative down. The negatives come from two sources:

More negatives per query means a stronger training signal, so a larger batch size directly improves training quality. Beyond that, the "cached" variant of the loss uses gradient caching to make large effective batch sizes feasible even when GPU memory is limited.

The mini_batch_size parameter controls how many samples are processed at once during the cached forward passes. For large multimodal models, setting this to a small value (e.g., 1) is important to avoid out-of-memory errors without sacrificing the benefits of large effective batch sizes:

To produce embeddings that work well at multiple dimensionalities, I wrap the base loss with MatryoshkaLoss. This trains the model so that truncating the embedding to a smaller number of dimensions still yields good performance:

This is especially useful for multimodal models, where embeddings can be large (2048 dimensions for Qwen3-VL). With Matryoshka training, you can use truncated embeddings (e.g., 256 or 128 dimensions) at deployment time for faster search with minimal quality loss. As I'll show in the Results section, the finetuned model achieves near-peak performance even at 512 dimensions.

The SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments class lets you control training hyperparameters. Here's the configuration used for the VDR finetuning:

A few things to note for (multimodal) training:

To track retrieval performance before, during, and after training, I use the InformationRetrievalEvaluator. It computes standard retrieval metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, and Recall@k:

The evaluator takes text queries, a corpus of images (including hard negatives), and a mapping of which documents are relevant to which queries. Note that the corpus contains a mix of positive and hard negative document screenshots, making this a challenging evaluation. Using batch_size=1 prevents out-of-memory issues during evaluation of the large VLM.

The SentenceTransformerTrainer brings everything together. Here's the complete training script:

The training script is nearly identical to a text-only training script. The only differences are:

Everything else (the trainer, training arguments, dataset loading) works exactly the same as text-only training.

After training for just 1 epoch, the finetuned tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 on the evaluation set (300 queries, 1500 corpus documents, cosine similarity). This is a significant improvement over the base Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models:

The finetuned 2B model outperforms even the 8B Qwen3-VL-Embedding model, demonstrating the power of task-specific finetuning. Finetuning on your own domain is often worth considering, even when a larger general-purpose model is available!

The comparison above uses full-size 2048-dim embeddings. Thanks to the Matryoshka training, the finetuned model also holds up well when truncated to fewer dimensions, letting you trade off embedding size and retrieval quality at deployment time:

The finetuned model's peak is at the full 2048 dimensions (0.948), but it stays within 0.3% of peak all the way down to 512 (4x smaller), and retains over 92% of peak even at 64 (32x smaller). Matryoshka training concentrates the most important information in the earlier dimensions, so moderate truncation costs very little performance.

The gap between 1024 and 2048 dimensions is small (0.946 vs. 0.948), so I've saved the model with truncate_dim=1024 set in its configuration. This means that SentenceTransformer("tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr") produces 1024-dimensional embeddings by default, halving the storage footprint compared to the full 2048. If you want a different dimensionality, pass truncate_dim=N when loading to override it.

You can also finetune multimodal Cross Encoder (reranker) models using the same training infrastructure. The key difference is using CrossEncoderTrainer and Cross Encoder-specific loss functions. This section provides a brief overview; see the full training examples for complete, runnable scripts with dataset preparation and evaluation.

Here's a simplified example based on the doodles training script, which trains a reranker to match images with text captions:

There are multiple valid architectural choices for multimodal rerankers, including:

Both approaches are demonstrated in the multimodal cross encoder training examples.

The two scripts linked above split the training data into two datasets, one per direction (image-to-text and text-to-image), with a task-specific prompt for each that tells the model how to score in that direction. Each positive pair is then expanded with randomly sampled negatives so the loss sees a balanced mix of matches and non-matches.

The Sentence Transformers repository includes several multimodal training examples:

#10196. Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec

For most of the last decade, an API call looked like a transaction. A client sent a request, waited, and got a complete response back in one piece. That model is exactly what most API management tooling — including API Gateway — was built to handle, and it still describes a huge amount of production traffic.

But that no longer describes all traffic types. A model generating a response emits tokens as it produces them, not in one batch at the end. An agent working through a multi-step task reports progress as it goes. A dashboard, a collaborative editor, a live inference endpoint — these all need a connection that stays open and carries data in both directions.

Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place. Teams ended up with a split estate — governed APIs on one path, ungoverned streaming traffic on another.

We're announcing that streaming support in API Gateway is available in Public Preview. Your streaming endpoints can now sit behind the same gateway, with the same policies, as everything else you serve.

For AI applications, streaming also strengthens API Gateway's connection to Gemini platform. A gateway that uses model routing now streams responses from Gemini, Claude and OpenAI gpt-oss models in model garden in Gemini platform as they're generated, and streaming backends you host anywhere else work the same way. Alongside Apigee and Agent Gateway in Gemini platform, API Gateway is the lightweight entry point to Google Cloud's AI gateway capabilities.

API Gateway now supports the full range of streaming patterns modern APIs rely on:

Streams can stay open for up to one hour. As with any long-lived connection, clients should implement reconnection logic so that a session survives the end of a stream — a well-behaved WebSocket or SSE client should be doing this anyway.

This is the part we are most pleased with: there is nothing new to learn.

Streaming is not a different product, a different resource type, or a different way of describing your API. There are no new extensions to add, no streaming-specific annotations, no separate spec for streaming operations. The same document that describes your existing API describes your streaming API.

Everything you already rely on continues to work exactly as before:

During Public Preview, you opt-in when creating the gateway:

That single flag is the entire difference. At GA, it is planned that streaming will simply be how API Gateway behaves, with no opt-in required and, as during Preview, no changes to your API config.

Alongside streaming, gateways get a deterministic default hostname:

Previously the default gateway.dev hostname included a generated hash, which meant you could not know your gateway's URL until after you had created it. That is a small thing that causes a lot of friction: you can't write the endpoint into a client config, a Terraform module, a CI pipeline, a firewall allowlist, or a partner integration doc until the resource exists — and if you tear the environment down and rebuild it, the URL changes underneath you.

Now the hostname is a pure function of values you already chose. You can generate it, template it, document it, and commit it to source control before the gateway exists, and you get the same URL every time you rebuild the same gateway in the same project and region. For anyone managing environments as code, or promoting a configuration from dev to staging to prod, this removes an entire category of bootstrapping problem.

Streaming isn't a niche feature for AI applications — it's the expected interaction pattern.

Users expect to see a model's response appear as it's generated, not after a thirty-second pause. Agents need to report intermediate steps. Tool-calling protocols and remote MCP servers depend on long-lived, incrementally-delivered connections. An API management layer that can't stream severely limits the user experience of AI applications.

With streaming, API Gateway becomes a viable front door for that agentic traffic — and the value of a front door is exactly the same as it's always been, only more urgent. AI endpoints are expensive, they consume quota, they need per-consumer authentication and rate limiting, and they need to be observable. These are the governance problems that an AI gateway is intended to solve. The alternative — every team standing up its own proxy in front of its own model endpoint — is how organizations end up unable to answer basic questions about who is calling what.

Model routing in API Gateway lets you expose a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and dispatch requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload. Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.

Streaming, model routing and MCP support are all features within API Gateway that provide a lightweight on-ramp to AI gateway capabilities within Google Cloud. These AI gateway capabilities allow teams to monitor, secure and control agentic traffic of tools, models and agents in their ecosystem, and they're delivered as a composable suite so you can choose the right gateway for each use case. For more expansive AI policies and full lifecycle management, use Apigee. To manage and secure agent connectivity, use Agent Gateway in Gemini platform. You can also combine these gateways: API Gateway or Apigee can sit in front of your agents and APIs, or behind Agent Gateway so your agents can reach models, tools, and MCP servers. For example, you can route your agent's egress through Agent Gateway for strict security governance, and then pass the request to API Gateway to handle model routing.

A few things to plan around while the feature is in Preview:

If you're already using API Gateway, the fastest way to see this working is to point a new streaming-enabled gateway at an existing backend that emits SSE and watch the events arrive incrementally. No spec changes needed.

#10194. The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the company’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

Still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

Just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

This display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

Oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

At $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually launched at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

If you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a big thumbs-up from me.

Lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon shows that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

We definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Big Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

DroidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

Now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

Obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

With all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

Scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app issues, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

You might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software update policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just said, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

We have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

#10192. The PR you would have opened yourself

Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness

We provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers. The Skill is designed to support contributors and reviewers as an aide, not an automation. We explain why we did it, how, and comment about how to meaningfully contribute to open source in the age of agents.

In 2026, code agents started to actually work. What used to be auto-completion at the side of your editor turned into a system that one-shots reasonable solutions from brief specifications. The generated code usually works out of the box, covers what you asked for, and makes reasonable assumptions about details you didn't specify. This is great. As Jensen Huang puts it, we've instantly gone from 30 million to one billion coders in the world. Creative minds are unleashed.

Take the transformers library as an example. It has hundreds of contributors, is used in thousands of projects, has been downloaded over a billion times. Suddenly, anyone with an agent can instruct it to find some open issue, fix it, and submit a PR. And that's exactly what's happening. Those people feel happy because they are contributing to a great library, but the sad reality is that, most of the time, they don't realize they are not.

Why not? There are two assumptions that agent-generated PRs usually miss.

Codebases like transformers care deeply about the code. It's cool to build projects where it doesn't matter what the code looks like, but transformers is not one of them. Being used by thousands of people, transformers is primarily built as a human-to-human communication method, through code. Model files read top to bottom, because we want practitioners to understand them without jumping through complex abstractions. This permeates throughout the library design and is the reason why, for example, we favor flat hierarchies.

Agents don't have that context. Because design decisions are not explicit, agents suggest refactors to "improve" the codebase by following "best practices", without realizing they are breaking implicit contracts between the library and its users. They are verbose, generalize too early, don't notice when a change affects other areas, introduce subtle bugs, break performance. They are also sycophantic, and accept any idea as good and follow it through diligently, including ones a maintainer would have pushed back early on with a terse comment.

A small number of maintainers still has to read every PR, understand it, decide if the design direction is right, identify side effects, and write feedback. PR volume has gone up tenfold, but the amount of maintainers has not (and cannot, because team coordination does not scale).

Transformers is one of the first projects to feel this pressure because of sheer volume, but the same dynamic is happening everywhere. As an example from a different domain, App Store reviewers are swamped because anyone can now build and submit an app, so many do.

The same logic applies to MLX: their maintainers care deeply about the code and read every PR carefully. We wanted to see whether agents could help contributors land high-quality model ports fast, and at the same time support reviewers in their work. Not only do we aspire to produce PRs that could have come from a careful human submission, but we also provide additional artifacts to increase the signal: generation examples, numerical comparisons, and a separate non-agentic test harness for reproducibility.

Another connection between transformers and MLX is that, most times, mlx-lm models are ported from transformers implementations. Because transformers focuses on clarity and readability, it has become the source of truth for model definitions. Downstream contributors wait until the transformers implementations are ready before they port to other frameworks. As a side effect, this is an excellent environment for an agent because it naturally limits the scope: rather than creating an implementation from scratch, the agent relies on transformers code as the source of truth.

This approach supports our goal: when a model lands in transformers, it should be available on MLX shortly after.

We built a Skill that mlx-lm contributors can use to port a model from transformers to MLX. Given a prompt like "convert the olmo_hybrid architecture to MLX", the Skill sets up a virtual environment to work on, discovers and downloads the relevant models from the Hub, reads the transformers modeling code, writes the MLX implementation, and runs a battery of tests. If results don't look right, it debugs and iterates, and does not declare success until it's satisfied.

We designed it to be useful to reviewers as much as contributors.

For the contributor, the Skill of course handles all the scaffolding: finding model variants on the Hub, diffing their configs to spot parameters that vary across model variants, downloading checkpoints, setting up editable installs of both mlx-lm and transformers. But it also handles the more difficult modeling tasks. It pays attention to salient architecture details and verifies sensitive areas, like RoPE configurations, that may result in hard-to-find bugs. It detects when the config doesn't declare a dtype and infers it from the safetensors metadata header. It runs per-layer comparisons between transformers and MLX to pinpoint exactly where divergence occurs. These are the kinds of checks that only someone with porting experience would think to run.

For the reviewer, the Skill produces a PR that is upfront about being agent-assisted, but does look like a careful human submission. Reviewers will see that the code follows mlx-lm conventions: idiomatic solutions, no unnecessary comments, no speculative abstractions, no modifications to shared utilities without explicit approval. Given that the code is agent-assisted, we try to include more data than the median PR, to provide as much signal as possible. The PR body includes a report with a summary of the variants and their architectural differences, generation examples, numerical comparisons, dtype verification, per-layer comparisons against the transformers baseline. The PR always discloses that it was agent-assisted, and the Skill will not open it until the contributor has accepted the results.

For verification, the Skill generates a test manifest for a separate, non-agentic test harness that is, by design, easily reproducible and not subject to LLM hallucinations or complacency (more on this below).

Skills are recipes for agents: simple text files with guidelines that steer the model through a complex task. They are not magic; you can achieve the same results via prompting and iteration. But they provide consistency (every run follows the same process, whereas different people would prompt differently), minimize ambiguity and serve as documentation: anyone can read the Skill to understand what it does, identify missing cases and suggest improvements.

We bootstrapped the Skill by porting a model ourselves, in conversation with Claude. I asked it to port GLM 4.7 from transformers to mlx-lm, giving instructions as I would during a normal session. One trick: I pointed Claude at a checkout of mlx-lm from which I had deleted the already-existing implementation, so I could compare the output against the ground truth. After a few iterations I had a working implementation, a conversation that revealed how Claude approached the problem, and the first draft of the Skill, which Claude created as a summary of the process. I edited it heavily, and incorporated the learnings from @gabegoodhart, who kindly shared their own porting conversation for a different model 🙌.

We repeated this loop several times and the Skill grew. On the technical side, we covered stuff such as RoPE bugs that may produce plausible output that degrades with long sequences, float32 precision contamination that silently kills inference speed (you'd be surprised how frequently these things happen!), config fields that vary across model variants in ways the implementation must handle, distributed inference for super large models that don't fit on a single machine. We taught it how to invoke the hf CLI to discover and download models. Most importantly, we instructed it to run the tests that experienced porters would, and to not declare success until they pass.

On the cultural side, we covered softer characteristics and explained the conventions that make a PR easy to review: don't use comments to explain code (the reviewer has to parse the comment and the code 🤦‍♂️), never propose refactors, don't touch shared utilities without asking. These rules cost the agent nothing but save the reviewer lots of time.

The end result: the contributor types a prompt, and the Skill produces a PR like this one, plus a test manifest for the external test harness.

The Skill shares a comprehensive results report as part of the PR. All these come from tests the agent runs during conversion, but we didn't want the reviewer to take a leap of faith to accept them. To go a step forward, we created a separate, non-agentic test harness that runs systematic tests on the converted code. This brings a couple of benefits:

The test harness is not a CI gate. Some checks are straightforward (is the output dtype correct?), but most are qualitative. Is it normal that a pre-trained model repeats itself in long sequences? Is a 4% relative logits difference against the transformers baseline acceptable? These are judgement calls based on experience with similar architectures. The harness provides useful signal, but it's the reviewer and contributor who still have to make the call.

The Skill is designed for the people who are already opening mlx-lm model PRs, or who would do it manually on their own. It's not meant for mass consumption, because PRs to mlx-lm are rarely accepted on sight. The typical cycle is: contributor opens a PR, reviewers point out improvements, both sides iterate until the quality bar is met. If this is true for expert submissions, it will remain true for agent-assisted ones.

If you're not prepared to engage in that cycle, you probably shouldn't be opening a PR. The reviewers will make an effort to understand your code (even knowing it was agent-assisted), so you should do the same. Own the code, and be ready to incorporate their feedback. In particular, don't hand reviewer comments back to an agent and post whatever it produces. LLMs double down on their decisions, go on tangents, and don't push back effectively. Once you engage with the reviewer, this becomes a person-to-person conversation, so it's your turn to discuss and be respectful of the time they put in.

You can also use the Skill to learn; you don't need to submit anything until your confidence and experience build. Read the Skill to identify problem areas you weren't aware of: it contains nearly 15 thousand words among the skill file, reference docs and utility scripts. Point it to your own fork of mlx-lm, try a conversion, and compare your output against the accepted implementation once it lands in the official repo. If you do this a few times, you'll learn a lot about transformers, MLX, and language model architectures.

We developed and tested the Skill using Claude Code. The same approach would work with Codex or other coding agents, but we haven't tested them. If you try the Skill in a different environment, please let us know how it goes!

The Skill works well for LLMs in mlx-lm, but there's plenty of room to grow.

The bottleneck in open source is not typing speed: it's understaning the codebase to change it without breaking the implicit and explicit contracts with users. Agents can help in this process, if we teach them what matters. We explored what this looks like in the context of mlx-lm, and hope it's useful for contributors and reviewers to land high-quality model conversions faster!

Thanks a lot to Ben, Shaun, Aritra for reading previous versions of this post and making it so much better 🙌

We are incredibly indebted to Apple for making MLX an open-source project, and to the community for instantly recognizing its value and contributing enthusiastically 🙏

#10190. The iPhone Duo’s rocky launch is a reminder of how far Android foldables have come

Good morning. Today I’m finding open source alternatives to all of my apps, poring through Pitchfork’s list of the 100 best indie rock albums to find ones I haven’t listened to, and preparing my body for November 19th by pre-loading GTA VI (and replaying GTA IV in the meantime).

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

On Monday, I unboxed the iPhone Duo I pre-ordered back in October and experienced a disarming sense of déjà vu. It’s beautiful hardware married to a messy, often painful software onboarding experience atypical of Apple’s usual polish. It reminds me of the Galaxy Fold’s early years.

I was most looking forward to the combination of a foldable form factor and Apple’s superior app ecosystem, but even the apps that have been updated to support the new aspect ratio, on both the front and back, feel ungainly and buggy. In moving UI elements from the bottom to the right, even with the display open, the Duo forces a rebuilding of essential muscle memory that’s prevailed across mobile platforms, including Android foldables, for 20 years.

The front display, in particular, is a massive test of one’s patience: apps, even ones ostensibly optimized for its stout dimensions, often feel unusable, with UI elements that would be prominent on the iPhone 18 Pro hidden behind overflow menus on the Duo. It’s exasperating and, frankly, boggling.

But what’s interesting is the enthusiasm with which developers are approaching the new form factor. Reddit threads reveal dozens of Duo-optimized app recommendations that feel novel and, if not polished, then propulsive. There’s a fascinating delta between waiting for my bank, or Starbucks, or Kobo, to get its act together to support the Duo and seeking out net-new opportunities and experiences.

I spent most of the summer using the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and I didn’t expect going back to it to feel so stately and predictable: the showcase of a platform with fewer highs but none of the Duo’s current lows.

I’m not sure if I’m going to keep the Duo and wait out its colicky infancy. But I do know that until now I hadn’t given Samsung enough credit for the amount of work it did to make foldable software feel ordinary, and that’s the highest compliment I can pay.

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Andrew’s look at the Boox Picco is a nice reminder that a gadget can be interesting because it does less. The $109 e-reader has a 4-inch screen, physical page-turn buttons, and an included magnetic case that can attach to a compatible phone. It competes directly with XTEINK’s excellent X4 Pro, which features a rudimentary touchscreen and backlight for around $100, though its magnets are built in.

Both products are wonderful examples of hardware companies adapting to the growing size and complexity of smartphones and seeing an opening for single-purpose products that do one thing really well. Plus, it’s fun to stick a thing to the back of your phone and… read it.

For something you can explore without buying another device, Paolo Mainardi turned his personal website into a point-and-click adventure. Articles live in books, links sit on a notice board, and his about page is a letter in a lighthouse. The Context Island is an incredibly thoughtful and unique approach to “web” design, and it’s another example of how AI can really help bring crazy ideas to fruition.

We’ll likely find out today whether Jensen Huang will be removed as Nvidia’s CEO. According to the WSJ, the company’s board is preparing to oust the company’s singular chief executive, who co-founded it in 1993.

Momentum picked up after the New York Times reported that in addition to his three-year affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, Jensen had a relationship with one of his direct reports, who still works at the company.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Tuesday.

#10188. Building Reliable Product Emails Into Your Application

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A password reset email is part of your login flow. An invoice notification is part of your billing experience. Yet development teams often treat these messages as background tasks: render a template, call a sending API, and move on. That approach leaves an important part of the product experience untested until a user cannot complete the action they started.

Testing the application interface alone leaves a gap. A successful request to an email provider does not establish that the recipient can find the message, understand it, or use its links. Product emails need explicit success criteria, useful diagnostic records, and recovery options when something fails.

A reliable workflow combines application tests, controlled mailbox checks, and pre-send diagnostics for authentication and inbox placement. A comparison of available tools can help you identify which checks your existing setup covers and where additional testing would be useful. The goal is to investigate specific gaps rather than add another service without a clear purpose.

Start with the action the recipient needs to complete. A weekly activity summary can tolerate a delay that would make a sign-in code useless. An invoice needs accurate amounts and a clear payment destination. A security alert needs enough context for someone to recognize the event without exposing sensitive information.

For each message, document its trigger, expected timing, required data, and expiration behavior. Decide what the application should display if submission fails or the user requests another copy. These decisions give developers and testers concrete acceptance criteria.

For a password reset, test the complete journey: requesting the message, receiving it in a controlled mailbox, following the link, and setting a new password. Also check what happens when the link expires or has already been used.

Template tests should cover the data your application actually encounters. Try long names, missing optional fields, non-Latin characters, and large order totals. Escape user-provided values appropriately, and make sure conditional sections disappear cleanly when their data is absent.

Inspect both HTML and plain-text versions. Instructions should remain understandable when images are blocked, while descriptive links and readable text should make the next action clear. Check that every URL points to the correct environment, especially when staging and production share template code.

A development sandbox lets you inspect generated messages without contacting customers. Use it to check headers, attachments, and content. Keep a separate rendering check for the email clients your audience uses, because a sandbox preview cannot reproduce every client’s behavior.

A background queue can prevent a slow sending API from delaying a web request. It also creates another failure boundary: a worker may time out after the provider has accepted the email but before your application records the result.

If the job retries blindly, the recipient may receive two messages. Assign a stable identifier to each logical notification and record the provider’s message identifier when available. Where supported, reuse an idempotency key for retries of the same send operation, following the provider’s documented retention window.

Distinguish retries from intentional resends. A user asking for a new reset link is a different event from a worker repeating an uncertain request. Define which link remains valid when another is issued, and test that behavior explicitly.

Retries also need limits. Temporary service failures may justify another attempt with backoff. A permanently invalid address needs a correction or suppression workflow, rather than repeated sending.

Provider events describe different stages of the sending process. An acceptance response means the provider accepted the request. A delivery event generally means the receiving mail server accepted the message; it does not prove inbox placement or that a person read it.

Capture the events your provider exposes, including bounces, delays, and complaints. Associate them with the original notification so support staff can investigate a particular report. Confirm each event’s documented meaning instead of treating similar labels across providers as interchangeable.

Webhook handlers should verify incoming requests using the provider’s documented mechanism and tolerate duplicate notifications. Avoid assuming events always arrive in chronological order. Record enough history to explain what happened without allowing a late event to overwrite a more informative state.

Before releasing a significant template or infrastructure change, send controlled messages through the production sending configuration to test accounts at commonly used mailbox providers. Use synthetic data, and check placement, rendering, link behavior, and how long the message takes to arrive.

Inspect authentication results in the received headers. Published DNS records are only part of the configuration; the actual message must use the expected signing domain and sending infrastructure. If you change providers or domains, repeat these checks rather than assuming the previous results still apply.

Treat test mailbox results as samples. They can reveal problems, but they cannot guarantee identical placement for every recipient. Mailbox settings, filtering decisions, and recipient history can produce different outcomes.

Provide a resend option with sensible rate limits and explain when users should expect the message. Where appropriate, let signed-in users verify or correct their address. For public account-recovery forms, avoid responses that reveal whether a particular address has an account.

Give support staff a way to distinguish a notification that was never generated from a failed submission or a message accepted by the receiving server. Protect that diagnostic access, limit retention, and avoid logging reset tokens, private message bodies, or unnecessary personal information.

Reliable product email depends on the whole journey, from the triggering event to the recipient’s next action. Testing each stage and making failures observable helps teams resolve problems before users repeatedly click resend or abandon the task.

#10187. Ecom-RLVE: Adaptive Verifiable Environments for E-Commerce Conversational Agents

TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations. EcomRLVE-GYM provides 8 verifiable environments — product discovery, substitution, cart building, returns, order tracking, policy QA, bundle planning, and multi-intent journeys — each with procedural problem generation, a 12-axis difficulty curriculum, and algorithmically verifiable rewards. We train a Qwen 3 8B model with DAPO over 300 steps and present early results demonstrating that environment scaling and adaptive difficulty transfer to agentic, real-world task completion.

This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥

Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion. A customer who asks "find me a USB-C charger under $25 that ships in two days" needs an agent that invokes the right catalog search, filters on three hard constraints, avoids hallucinating product IDs it never retrieved, and handles follow-ups when the top result goes out of stock.

Supervised fine-tuning can teach surface-level tool use from demonstrations, but it cannot scale to the combinatorial space of constraint configurations, partial-information dialogues, and multi-step transactional workflows that real e-commerce demands.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers an alternative: the agent optimises for outcomes — did the products satisfy the constraints? Was the cart correct? Was the return initiated for the right order line? The challenge is constructing reward functions that are both verifiable (no LLM-as-a-judge subjectivity) and adaptive (difficulty that grows with the policy's capability).

RLVE-Gym provides 400 environments for sorting, multiplication, Sudoku, and other algorithmic-reasoning tasks; however, those are all single-turn, text-in / text-out puzzles — extending to agentic domains was left as future work.

EcomRLVE-GYM fills that gap: we stay in the verifiable regime (e-commerce outcomes can be checked algorithmically) while extending to multi-turn, tool-augmented, agentic conversations — environments where the agent must act (call tools, modify world state) rather than merely reason (produce a text answer) and compensates for the deficiency of the search system.

EcomRLVE-GYM transforms customer-service outcomes structurally verifiable:

Every signal above can be evaluated by a program with access to the hidden ground-truth goal. No human annotation or LLM-as-a-judge is needed.

Before we explain the framework, here is what a single EcomRLVE episode looks like at difficulty d = 4. The environment generates a hidden goal, a simulated user opens the chat, and the agent must use tools to satisfy the request. Every action is verified algorithmically — no LLM judge required.

The reward is fully computed by code: F1 over (product, variant, qty) tuples, an efficiency bonus for finishing in fewer turns, and a hallucination check that every recommended product ID was actually retrieved. If the agent had picked the Lightning variant instead of USB-C, the simulated user would have corrected it mid-dialogue — and the F1 would have dropped.

Each environment covers a distinct real-world shopping scenario. The agent must complete the task using tools (catalog search, cart operations, order lookups, policy queries) and is scored by a program — not a human or another LLM.

Every environment uses the same three-part reward signal:

Invalid outputs (malformed JSON, illegal tool calls) trigger an immediate failure score, creating a strong incentive for well-formed responses from step one.

A single difficulty number d controls 12 independent aspects of a task simultaneously. This is important because e-commerce conversations are hard in many different ways at once — not just along one dimension.

Here are four representative difficulty axes:

The other eight axes cover turn budget, input noise (typos, slang), context switches, retrieval depth, order-history size, policy complexity, and tool budget. The full breakdown is in the technical report.

Adaptive scheduling. Each environment tracks the agent's success rate independently and only advances to harder problems once the agent is passing the current level reliably. This keeps every environment training at the agent's capability frontier — avoiding both "too easy to learn from" and "too hard to make progress on".

Cart building is a good showcase because it requires the full search → inspect → clarify → act loop, has a binary ground truth, and introduces a challenge absent from most recommendation benchmarks: variant selection.

To succeed, the agent must develop five distinct skills:

The agent uses six tools to accomplish this:

The generator samples 1–5 target products (scaling in difficulty with d), each potentially requiring a specific variant (USB-C vs Lightning, Matte vs Glossy) and a quantity > 1. The agent must:

Real product catalogs have sparse variant data — many products have none, and those that do typically vary only by colour or size. To create a richer discrimination task, we synthesize variants at episode initialization:

At d = 0 the agent adds a single product with no variant complexity — learning the basic catalog.search → cart.add workflow. At d = 6 it juggles 3 items, nearly all requiring a specific variant, with half needing qty > 1.

The cart must be exactly right — correct product, correct variant, correct quantity. Partial credit is given for partially correct carts, but a perfect score requires every item to match. If the agent adds the wrong variant, the simulated user corrects it mid-dialogue ("that's the Lightning version, but I need USB-C"), giving the agent a chance to self-correct before the episode ends.

Two real E_CART episodes from a Qwen 3 8B agent. Same environment, same agent — difficulty alone changes the game.

At d=1 the agent solves the task in 3 clean turns. At d=8 it spirals — picking Bamboo instead of Charcoal, XL instead of XS, never fixing the air fryer despite two user corrections, then hallucinating that the variant doesn't exist. This is exactly the kind of multi-step error cascade that the difficulty curriculum surfaces, and that adaptive training should teach the agent to recover from.

A verifiable environment needs a user simulator that behaves realistically. We use Qwen3.5 (9.7B) to generate natural, varied user messages rather than canned templates — covering everything from typo-filled requests to mid-conversation topic switches.

Two design choices matter for training quality:

Preferences match stated constraints. Each simulated user has a hidden set of preferences (price sensitivity, brand loyalty, shipping speed, etc.). These are deliberately biased toward whatever constraints the user communicated — so if the user said "under $25", the reward function actually cares about price. Without this, an agent could be penalised for correctly following the user's instructions.

Strategic omission. The LLM deliberately withholds some constraints from the opening message to force the agent to ask clarifying questions. The system tracks exactly what was and wasn't mentioned, so the agent is never penalised for information it was never given.

Following RLVE's methodology, we define nested environment collections:

We hypothesise — consistent with RLVE's findings — that C8 agents outperform single-environment specialists, even on the specialist's own task.

We trained Qwen 3 8B with DAPO on C1 (Cart Building) for 300 steps as an initial viability study.

We saw progressive growth in difficulty reached, confirming that adaptive scheduling produces a steady learning signal rather than the saturation (static-low) or starvation (static-high) patterns predicted by the RLVE paper.

#10185. Google launches Intelligent Eyewear glasses: $395+, pre-order today, ships Dec. 10

After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly.

There is a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera for photos and videos (3K 30FPS or 1080p). You get image stabilization and HDR processing, while four microphones work to provide spatial audio capture. Google is also quite proud of its noise cancellation work.

There are two open-ear speakers for balanced audio and clear vocals. Control is done by a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes, or via voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword.

Another way to control Intelligent Eyewear is through your Pixel Watch or Galaxy Watch, with Fitbit Air support coming next year:

Notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. These visuals won’t be used to train AI models or for ad targeting. Additionally, the glasses will “automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them.”

Battery life (245mAh) is rated at nine hours on a single charge, with a fully topped-up charging case (Gentle Monster’s shown below) offering seven full charges. Power is transferred via contact pins located on the underside of the nose bridge.

Android XR runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. Other specifications include Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 6E, and IPX4 water resistance. Samsung is responsible for engineering the hardware, while there are two eyewear brands at launch.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

These glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:

Pre-orders for Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear start today with retail availability on December 10.

#10183. Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

Google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

As a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

The sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how big a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

There is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

From its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

Talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

That indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

Under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal issues. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.
